blocks.x: I'll give you a full name if you will.
My name is Lace Hall Nelson Senior, 1419 Two Row Street, New Orleans, Louisiana.
Where were you born? What part of the town were you born in?
I was born right here at 1419 Two Row Street.
Right in the same house?
In the same house, yes sir.
Your father was Dr. Nelson. You might tell a little bit about your parents if you will.

Well, when I was a baby about two months old, my daddy left me and he went out to a country town by the name of the family. He went out to a country town by the name of Napoleonville, Louisiana. And he practiced medicine out there. And we stayed out there for about 25 years or more. And I moved back down to New Orleans.
If you don't mind, would you give your birth date just when you were born?
September 17th, 1902.
1902. You once told me your mother played piano. Yes, she did. Would you tell us a little about her?

Yes, she did. Her home is in Springfield, Massachusetts. And she finished from the Boston Conservatory of Music. And by her being such a wonderful piano player and musician, I just picked up the talent, you understand? And I teach with Professor Claiborne Williams of Donaldsonville, Louisiana.
Was he down here? Where did you study with him?
Out in Napoleonville. He was living in Donaldsonville. At that time? That's only a 12 miles distance.
What was your first instrument? Was the trombone the first?
No, I started playing on altos. One of those straight altos, you know? Altos. I started poop, poop, peck, peck on, as they called it. You understand? And from then, then I took up—
How old were you about?

Oh, I imagine I was about 16, something like that, around that neighborhood. And they had a fellow out there, I forget his name, but we used to call him Cousin Lawrence. He left with a fellow by the name of Paul Jones. They left there and they went to Shrekeport. And he had a wonderful brass band out there, I forget the name of it. And I always admired that man's trombone player, and he was a wonderful trombone player. So I said, one of these days I'm going to try to be a trombone player like my cousin. So from then on I just went to the old Sliphorn and got Professor Clevon Williams to come down to teach me. And when he taught me, when he was teaching me rather, he taught me the man, you know, taking the breaths. That's the principal part of it, you understand? The breathing. And then from then on I just felt like I knew enough. And I just joined up with a band, a fellow by the name of George Nelson. We had a little band in the point with a little six piece combination, you understand?
Any relation? No, no relation at all.

He was what you call a fellow, he couldn't see at night but he could just make out in the day. And he was a wonderful violin player. He used to come by my mother when we'd get new music like that. She'd play the melody on the piano and he had a real good ear, but he couldn't see the music at all. But he was a fine fellow. And then from there I played a couple of dates with Professor Clevon Williams and his band. Then later on, after I married, my son was born, I played with a fellow in Tippet-Owe by the name of Joseph Gabriel. They call him Gabriel, but some people say Gabriel, but we call him Gabriel. He was also, he had about a ten piece orchestra. He used to play all down by a place named Luke. He played at the big pavilion in Homer. Well, he had quite a bit of work. He kept me going Wednesdays, Thursdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays.
Do you remember Lewis James, the bass player? Sure, sure. Was he from there? I think he told us.

He's from Tippet-Owe. He had Lewis James and he had two other brothers. One played clarinet. Well, you know Lewis James instrument was tenor sax and clarinet. Yes. And he just, I think he just got on the bass since he came here in New Orleans.
Yes, I believe he told us about these Gabriel.

Yeah, and then he had another brother named Pallet. He was a trombone player and he went to the bass. Then he had another brother named Willie. Well, he played saxophone and clarinet. They all used to play with Joe Gabriel, but they had some kind of falling out and they organized the James brothers band out there in Tippet-Owe. And then from there I came down to New Orleans.
Well, how old were you when you got your trombone about?
Oh, I'd say about twenty.
Not until twenty.
Yeah, and I came down here to New Orleans and I got with a fellow by the name of Kit Harris. You might have heard of him.
Oh yes, the trumpet player?
Yeah, he's dead now.
I'd like to ask a little bit more though about those older days, about Claiborne Williams since we never got to talk to him. What did he play? What was his main instrument?
Well, Professor Claiborne Williams, he was a violin player, but he used to teach all instruments.
He taught all of them.
Trombone, trumpet, clarinet, sax, piano, bass, just any instrument. He knew them all.
Do you remember what method you learned from him? No. The music you used or anything?
No.
I'd like to find out all those little details you know about because we never got to talk to him.
Well, the name of that method, I couldn't tell you that, Mr. Moore.
Did you hear his band? How did his band play? Oh, he had a wonderful band.

Professor Claiborne Williams had a wonderful band. He came down here to New Orleans and he played on the Pelican roof garden there when it was open. And you couldn't get in there. The people here in New Orleans say that all the larger bands from the north came down and say, but Professor Williams, he really played music.
How big was his band?

I imagine about sixteen pieces. Big band. Oh yeah, it was a large band, yes sir. He had a brother, he used to play trombone but he died. He used to play in that high register all the time. He thought there was a trumpet playing all the time. He died of consumption.
There was one Williams that went up with Handy and played with him. Do you know if it was a man that traveled with?

No, I couldn't say it. Only William I know as Professor Williams and his brother played bass and his son George. I think he's now in Baton Rouge. He has an orchestra out of Baton Rouge. What type of music did they use? Were they everything arranged? That is they used the music?

No, they just used orchestration. Well a few arrangements, not too many. Reginald stock arrangements? Just stock, regular stock, yes sir. Reginald stock arrangements. And to tell you I came here and I played with Kit Harris.

And when I was playing with Kit Harris, a fellow by the name of Eugene Ware, he was a trumpet player in the Desvene's orchestra. And he came up there to hear us one night rehearsal and Desvene at that particular time he needed a trombone player. And Mr. Ware must have went and told Desvene that if you want a good trombone player you can get him one. So after I lost my wife, I waited a year and I happened to go by the Bulls, you know where that is. Bulls uptown. And this fellow Ware saw me and he called me. And Sidney asked me was I doing anything and I told him no. So he said be out on the, I forget the name of that boat, no it wasn't the captain. Sidney New Orleans, be out there for rehearsal. So I went out there that Tuesday and I made rehearsal and then I got with Sidney Desvene's orchestra. I played with him for a number of years. What line was it?
Was that the Streckfus line?
That's the Streckfus line. The Streckfus line. And after they discarded the city of New Orleans then the capital took its place.
You don't remember the city of New Orleans.

You don't. Then they had another boat we used to have, it was a colored excursion boat, it used to be at the foot of Napoleon Avenue called Idlewild. We played on that for a couple of weeks. And then we went up the river. Was that just for colored then? Just for colored, that boat up at Napoleon Avenue, yes. And then we went, used to go up the river as far as St. Paul, Minnesota every year for about five or six years.
Who else was in the band?
Oh the names, it's pretty hard for me to remember all those fellas. I can give you a few.
Any other trombone or trumpet player besides Sidney that you remember?
Eugene Ware and George Flemons. And they had Lewis Bobberin on drum. They had Ransom Norlins on bass. One year we used Loving Good. Another year we used Steve J. Lewis. And another year we used-
It was on Deanna, Steve Lewis.
Yeah, and then we used Professor Blanchett.
Oh yeah.
And we had, I just remember that guitar player, it was Rene Hall. Then we had Adolf Alexander on sax, Theodore Poinel, and Sam Dutre on tenor.
Was that young Sam Dutre or the old man?

The young Sam Dutre. The big fella, yeah. The young Sam Dutre. The big fella, yeah. The young Sam Dutre. And then after we finished playing on the captive, then we came out in the city. And we played for all the leading hotels in the city of New Orleans and all the restaurants, La Lusanne and all different, all those big high class restaurants, Sun Yacht Club, Jewish Country Club, Metric Country Club, and all those places like that. We only played one night a week for Colette and that was on the roof guard and that was every Monday night. We had that engagement.
Was that the Pelican or the other Pythian Temple?
That's the Pythian Temple. We called it the old roof guard. Yeah. Yeah.
I was going to ask some more about that Idlewild. I think I saw a picture, Idlewild or what? Well it didn't stay here long.
How big was it?
Oh, a good size boat.
About as big as the capital?
No, not quite that large. Was it a side wheeler or back? No, back stern wheeler.
Stern wheeler.
That's a stern wheeler, yes.
Made like the capital, not as large.
Yeah, big dance floor and all the other. Big dance floor and everything.

Then I went up the river one year on President out there now. We made a trip up there. For one year, didn't go no footer to St. Louis. Then we made a trip, I made a trip up the river with him on the Island of Queen. Well the weather was so bad we couldn't get no footer than Memphis. As far as he could go, it was too cold.
Is that the boat that went up the Ohio sometimes? That's the boat.
Used to go to Cincinnati.
Yeah.
Well I wasn't with him when he was on that boat going to Cincinnati. See, he had a fellow by the name of Oil Umphrey. If you remember him. That's Willie Umphrey's brother.
Boyce Umphrey's brother.
He's a trombone player. Well the reason why he left Sydney, not to say his musical ability, he's a circus man. He likes to follow the shows. He don't stay in one place, he likes to travel.
He's over in Virginia now, someplace based.
I don't know. He does? Well I don't know, I couldn't tell you, I don't know where he passed. I couldn't tell you that.
No he's still there. His brother's over.
He is. Uh huh. Then I played with Buddy Petit. I played with Rene.
Well let's talk about Buddy Petit for a minute. What kind of a band did he have? How big or?
Oh no more than about a seven piece. Sammy Penn used to play with him too.
That's right, we'll talk to him tomorrow night.
Uh huh.

I played with Rene. Well let's talk about, I don't want to keep interrupting you. That's alright. Did you all use music? How was Buddy Petit? Was he a good reader or a good musician? What did you think of him?

Well he could read, what do you say, spell you know, but mostly head music. He was head arranging. Yeah he was head arranging. He started off, you know, go play Donna, da da da, and give you the cue and then go ahead and go play Shine, da da da, and then just go ahead and we just knock off and just go on. Who else was in the band with you there? Nah I can't remember those fellas names. Was Sammy with you at the same time?
Yes he was there, yeah. He may remember a couple of them too.

Yeah Sammy no one better than me. I played just a set in for a couple of nights, a couple of jobs with him, you understand? I wasn't a regular man but Sammy was with him longer than I was. What kind of a band was it to play with, Lewis? What do you mean? Was it an easy band to play with? Who Buddy Petit? Oh yeah. Just the same as Thomas, the same thing.

Same thing. What kind of a style did he have on trumpet? Is it like anybody we know now around, like say Kid Thomas or Armstrong? No, he was more close to Louis Armstrong. Yeah he was pretty close to Louis Armstrong. If he'd have lived the day, he'd have been on Bowie Street, I believe in the city of Papacillistan because he had a better pull here than Cillistan in those days.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Now Punch when I was playing with him he used to use a water bucket, you understand, when he was playing. My little Margie would take a water bucket and play in the thing.
He never used his hand or anything?

Oh yeah, it was the same thing, you know. Glasses, we got Coca Cola bottles, anything. Oh you did all that? Yeah, sure. Those times they had those big large crash timbers, you know, they hit it and let it ring. That drum on that going out chorus, you know.
Did Buddy Petit have a pretty big tone? Was he loud or solid?

Oh yeah, he was a powerful fellow. Yeah, a powerful fellow. You see in those times they used to call you, when you give a dance, like if you'd give a dance, like if it's going to be Saturday night, or Saturday in the day they'd call and make an advertisement. You'd get on the truck or the wagon, whatever it was, you understand, and go around and play. And when Buddy Petit and Rene would meet, that's it. Yeah, yeah, yeah, they'd go see who can out-blow each other. That was it right there. Surely.
You played with Kid Rene too then? I did, yeah, yes.
He was playing at the Levita. Yeah, he used to play at the Levita, the Levita dance hall. How was he?
What kind of a trumpet? Nice trumpet player too.
He wasn't too loud of a man, he was a soft type fellow. Make plenty of variations on his trumpet. He's a nice sweet trumpet player, he's a fine fellow.
Go ahead, Nancy, we'll turn it off. We were talking about Kid Rene. Yes sir. Some people told me he was specialized in high notes. Do you remember when you played with him? Was he a high notes man?
Yes, yes, at that particular time, yeah, when he was at the Levita. When he first started there he was a pretty high note man, but a job like that, Mr. Bill.
He's a taxi dance job.

Yeah, it's a gypsy dance they call it. You see, you start at 8 o'clock and you just continue. Piece after piece till 3 o'clock, 4 o'clock, 5 o'clock, 6 o'clock in the morning. I've come out that place sometimes 7 o'clock in the morning. Just continues to play all night, don't stop. The only time you stop for your lunch. And then the saxophone player, he got to stay there and play all the melody. Then when Rene would come back, the saxophone player would go eat. When the saxophone player would come back, the trombone player would go eat. You always need to do anything like that, you understand? I mean, it was a pretty rough job.
Yeah. Who else was in Kid Rene's band on that job, can you remember?
Oh, myself, Rene, probably they call it Sport, that's Young.
Oh, yes.

And his brother was on the bass. Walter Deco was on the piano. Now this fellow called Gaier, I don't know his name. All I know of him, remember he got, he met with a misfortune in the place. Yeah. Now the drummer, who did he, he had his brother on drums. I forget his brother's name. Joe Rene. Joe Rene, yeah, was playing drums. How was he?
A pretty good drummer? I never got to hear him play.
He was just a one beat drummer, you know. Just a one beat drummer.
Was he alright or anything special?
No, just kept straight timing, hit the cymbals, that's all.
Never got to hear him.
Never did, huh?

I didn't hear Kid Rene was, maybe his brother was with him down in the Cadillac, on St. Claude, way down in 1942, but he, that was near the end of his life, he wasn't playing so well then I guess. He seemed to be tired out that night. Any other small bands? Did you ever play with Chris Kelly, for instance?
I played with Chris Kelly, one job. One job, one job only, just one job, one night. Funny thing about it, I don't want to work with that fellow anymore.
Was he a tough one to work with?

Yeah, he was pretty tough, he was a good, he used to play the blues. Yeah, he used to play the blues. And I kept seeing him coming with the whiskey, you know, the whiskey and whiskey. When I asked for my money, he said, that's the money there, I drank it all up, no money. I don't want to see, I don't want to play with that fellow no more in my life. Played all night for whiskey and I wasn't drinking, I was just playing for them. I said, where the money? He said, that was the money there, all the empty bottles down there, that's the money, nothing.
And you weren't drinking?
No.
Where was the job, remember, what kind of a job?
Well we played in some big house when the sport, you know, the…
Oh, in the district?
In the district, yeah, when it was over running, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, we played in some big house.
Did you ever play in any other dance halls over in the district?
No, like what do you mean?
Well, like the Entertainer's 101 Ranch?
No, I didn't play in there.
Or Pete Lawless, I guess. I used to go there every night.

See, they had their own band there. All I can remember was, when Mr. Pena, he used to play drums and I didn't pay too much to the other people who was playing there. I used to go there every night and we'd knock off it, sit and stop by there, see what was going on.

When you were young, who were the best trombonists around town in the early days that you can remember? Hearing music? When did you move here? You didn't hear music much before you left town, I guess, here to go up to… How old were you when you went to Napoleonville? Oh, I was a baby.
Mr. Ben's what I thought.
Yeah. When did you move back here? Oh, let's see.

Moved back here, I imagine, about 1926. My daughter was born in 27, she was born here. My son was born in 25, he was born in the country. Now you ask me who was the best trombone player? No, that's pretty nice.
Or even up in the country, wherever you heard music.

I was the only trombone player out in that part. And they had a fellow, like I was telling you, Professor Claiborne Williams' brother, and they had another fellow there, the James boys, well he wasn't so much on trombone, he got off a bass to trombone, his instrument was bass. You understand?
Well can you remember your very first trombone where you got it, or what kind of a horn it was? Any special story about that, anything?

First trombone I got it was a busher. No, C.G. Kahn. You want the real first one? I got an old horn out from Donisonville, Professor Claiborne Williams sold me one. You got one from him. But when I came to New Orleans, when I got with Sidney Desby and I used that old horn, I traded it in, I went to Whirline and bought a C.G. Kahn. And after I used the Kahn a while, I went over to the busher. And that's the same instrument what I have there now.
Which make do you like best?

The busher is a pretty good instrument. Good horn. Yes sir. I had that Kahn, he had a small bow, but this busher, I bought a big bow and a large bell. Give you more volume. Yeah. I had people that make them trombone pairs like Mr. Pearson. He used to get those special mouthpieces with a small hole. That's how he could make those high notes, but he couldn't make the low ones. But I got just a regular, regular, regular sized mouthpiece. The mouthpiece that I got, he gave it to me, he didn't like it. Now I don't find no trouble with it, I haven't used that mouthpiece about ten years.
Sounds wonderful to me.
Yeah, surely. And I bought that horn from Morris Music. I was doing the WPA time and I was working on the WPA. I bought that horn from Morris.
Were you in that WPA band too?

I was in that, yes sir. Professor Martinez used to lead the band. And Lester Mayen was the leader when Martinez wasn't there. You know Mr. Martinez used to be piano player at the Sang-a-sale. He was a wonderful piano player. I saw some music that he wrote.
I picked up an old piece of sheet music that he wrote.

He kept us on, what he liked most, he didn't want that. He didn't want that old jazz, the orchestration when he'd had. He wanted to play all them overtures. He was crazy about that and we had to play all of that.
Was that mostly a big brass band? Big brass band.
When I first went in that band, Mr. Bill, once they had about twenty or more trombone players. They had Frankie Doocy, you remember him?
I didn't know him but I heard all about him.

He was number one trombone player. They had me way on the end. He was playing first parts, I was playing third, way around the end. People was coming with those old trombone cases, you know. You open the top and pull the horn out of that way. I've never seen so many instruments in all days of my life, funny instruments in all days of my life on that WPA band. So when we moved over to Tulane Club, they had an examination. You understand, Mr. Martinez and I happened to be, I happened to walk, he sent for me. I didn't know what he wanted, I left my horn at home. And I used another fella's trombone. I used Sonny Henry's trombone, one of them. And they put that piece on us, March Gloria. And he asked me what key it was in. And the tempo and all that. And he told me, you one of them smart fellas, go ahead and try it off.
I knocked the tempo off and he goes, da da da da da da da da da da da.

That's enough, take it down there. No other part is after the beats, no da da da da da. That's enough, get out of here. Then he called Franky Deuce and them fellas up there. When they wound up, they had five of us left. I was number one drummer with me. That's where he caught a wall and he thinned that band out. He brought it down to about 40 pieces. They must have had about 100 before he started. And he got it down to 40 pieces. Gilbert Young was in there. Oh, Sidney Montague. Frasier, Joshua Frasier there. Saeed they called him. Winner Stripanyan. Manuel Paul. Oh, some people out of Papa Celestan. Ricki Alexis. Louis DeMaine. Oh, there's people out there. I just can't place all the names. They had so many.
I saw a big picture of that. How long did you stay in that band then?
Well, I stayed until it went out of existence. I just remember how many years.
Yeah.
Until it went out of existence.
Did you play any dance jobs? Somebody told me they had some small dance groups in that big band too. Did they send out for dances or something?
No sir, I don't remember playing. I don't remember them having no dances. They did have some at the Tulane Club. But I never did play at them.
Is that where the Tulane Club is now?
Yes sir. We used to go to the palace prison once a week.
That's what I mean. I heard something about that. That was a whole band?
No he picked men to go back there.
Just a certain room smaller.

Pick his orchestra, he called it. He didn't pick the whole band. He had his men pick. He used to send me back there. Then we used to go out to the boys' home back out here on the Captain Jones. Played back there.
It was all marches and all overtures that were recorded?

Well he mixed them in. It was a few arrangements he had and overtures and marches and orchestrations. So not only jazz numbers especially, not for the big band? No, he didn't split the band for that, no sir.
I was going to ask some more about your mother too. She learned the piano. Where did she play? Did she ever teach music much?
Yes she taught out in Napoleonville, yes she did. As I said she finished from the Boston Conservatory of Music in Massachusetts, Boston, Massachusetts.
Did she play any concerts around any place? No she didn't.

She mostly donated her services to the church. She played the pipe organ. When they didn't have the organ, the pipe organ, she played the piano. And she taught school out in Napoleonville. She specializes in mathematics. Mathematician, you know. Music, if you don't know mathematics you're in bad shape because you've got plenty of adding, subtracting, and division in music. If you don't know if you're a bad mathematician you're in bad shape.
She only played classical music I suppose. Yes sir. Never playing jazz then? No sir, no, no jazz.
No sir.
Did she approve of you taking up any?

Yeah, she wanted me to play piano but I always did like trombos. After I heard that fellow say cousin Lawrence, I don't forget his last name. I wanted to be like him. She came to Whirline one day to buy a book, you know, to play, to practice at home, practicing on the piano. And she asked to click for one of those books and he'd go give her a little second grade. She said I don't want that, I want 12th grade. I said you know you can't play no 12th grade music. So she just opened the book and said have your piano player, I'd have to play this for me. The lady couldn't play it. She said you mind if I come sit down? She said the clerk said certainly. She went there and never seen it before and just went on and played it. Man, stood his mouth open, didn't know what to say. All right. Played it just like she, she says I beg your pardon later. I don't blame you for asking for this 12th grade music. She said do you have anything harder? He said no, that's as high as we have here. Well she's a wonderful piano player. When she was taught she said she had to, you know how to span them and they put a nickel on each wrist to keep and she played and let those nickels drop off. Just had to play that level, you understand? That's the way they taught her.
I haven't heard of that.
Yeah.
Was she from the south here or didn't she?
No sir, she was born in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Oh she was born in the-
Yes, she came south, that's how she met my father. She was teaching school out in Shreveport. And they happened to come here and I met and that's for my time.
Were there many colored doctors at the time your father started out? I wonder, where did he go to school? Do you remember anything about his? He went to Streets University.

Oh yes, I've heard of that. Yes, he went to Streets University. That's part of Dillard now, I think. And he was over here at Flint Goodies, he was on Canal Street, Canal and Robinson. I don't know if you don't remember that.
Oh I've heard of it though, I remember when it was there. It's now one up on Louisiana.
Yeah, and he taught Dr. Federicks, Rivers Federicks, that great colored surgeon area. He's dead now.
How old, when was your father born about? Do you know about?
Well, it's in 18, he's 88. So that's, it's 18, I just remember the date. The 1800s or not. Yeah. See he was the first lieutenant in the Spanish American War.
He was in that, I don't know. Oh yeah.
Fought on San Juan Hill over in Cuba. Talk to him about some of those old days too.
No, he don't hear, he don't see.
All he do is just sit over there in the room.
We wouldn't want to bother him, but he couldn't hear. It would have been nice if we had a few, ten years ago. Oh sure, oh yeah. When we used to record here.
Mm-hm, he's a 32nd degree mason too. Mm-hm. Know masonry too.
Well to make a note about that this is where you recorded that. Oh yeah this is the room where we recorded.
Yeah, sitting right over there. Yeah, big old.

Witten Joe was here one night. Austin Young, a lot of those fellows have gone on now. That's right. The drummer too, remember. What's the matter with me? I can't think of his name. You know, played with Big Eye.
I know you're speaking about that. I see him. He wait for the railroad. I see him every day. I can't call him.
Well, the child was here too. But I mean, who was the other drummer?
I can't place it.
Played with Big Eye. I can't... I'll think of his name in a minute. He died about four years ago.
Oh, he used to play with John Casimir Brass Band. Used to be a porter over there. Rogers. Rogers, that's right. That's right. Curtis Rogers. That's right. He was a custodian at the City Hall.
And Ann Cook, remember the night we recorded Ann Cook?
Yes, sir.
You had a piano here in those days. Right over here. Yeah. Is that your mother's old piano?
Yeah, she's been at that piano a long time. Yeah, a long time.

I was wondering if there's anything else you can tell about the, on the boats, anything particular? Do you remember about the bands on the boats? Were they mostly arrangements that you played all the time?
Well, Sidney was a man, he didn't believe in too many arrangements. He believed in stocks. Just ordinary stocks.
Just ordinary stocks. Just ordinary stocks.

And the captain on that boat, he's a very peculiar fella. He wants you to... He set the 10-4 for you. He'd get out there with his watch. He'd time you. He wanted... It's got to be just right. And you got 12 numbers to play a night, and you got to get them all in. That was one of the... That's Captain Roy's Streckfus. Roy's Streckfus. He had to take orders from his brother, Joe Streckfus. That's the man one. He stays in St. Louis. He don't come down there.
I remember Baby Dobbs, the drummer, told me about.

Yeah, very certainly. When that boat be coming, he be standing on that barge waiting. You see how it's going to land. And then he walk on, he send orders down there, and he'd look around, see if everything fixed just the way he ordered it. Well, it's a nice trip. It's the hardest part is going upstream, you see. You go so slow. Yeah. Then you make those stops. Coming down is all right. See, you're coming with the current.
Did you have any rehearsals in the morning or any time?
Yeah, we had to have rehearsals every Tuesday morning, 10 o'clock.
Once a week?

Once a week, every Tuesday morning, 10 o'clock. When we was in St. Paul, Minnesota, we had to be awake on the bandstand for 9.30 to start at 10. And we used to come down the rivers for us, Haston, Minnesota, to the locks, go through the locks, turn around and come back, and then get back to St. Paul, Minnesota, and land for 5 o'clock. And then be right back on the bandstand for 8, and knock off at 12. But when we was in St. Paul, he eliminated some of those rehearsals. Because that was too rough. Yeah. Every day, and we stayed with-
They played daytime excursions there too? Daytime and night. And night.
Night dancing. And we did that, we stayed there 11 months.
I mean 11 weeks.
11 weeks. 11 weeks.
11 weeks, yes.
In St. Paul.
In St. Paul. Was there much dancing in the daytime or did-
No, they didn't dance too much. But you did play, you had to play. We had to play, whether they danced or not. Yeah. We just had to play. But at night, nice crowds.

What did they pay on the boats, if you don't mind telling? Oh, they paid $25 a week. And you got your meals and the place to stay. In the middle, $25 a week. Board and large. And you went to a place like St. Paul for a while, did you sleep on the boat? Sleep on the boat, yeah.
Nice sleeping quarters. It was alright.
Eat and sleep right on the boat, yeah.
So it might be hot down in there some time.
No, on the upper deck.

That's on the capitol. Good breeze. But on the steam of presence, it's actually down in the hub. Yeah, you're down there. But the water keep you cool, you see. That's right. Did you play on the president here?
You're speaking about the president?
Yeah, we played about a week here and then she left.
On the president?
On this president here, yeah. Then she left and went to St. Louis. And we got off from St. Louis and they paid our trade fair back. I think she went up there for repairs or something.
Oh, I see, yeah.
They paid and sent us back on the trade.
Oh, he came back on the trade.
Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Did you work here in the wintertime on the boat then too, down here?
Well, we worked out there one year. For a few. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
You were talking about the breakfast lines, the boats, and when you played here. Did the boats, the same boat that stayed here in the wintertime, did it go upstream then in the summer?
Yes, the steamer capital, it worked here all winter. Then in the summer it would go up to St. Paul. And then returning and then Wake Will and Sam Heiserbois.
Do you remember who played the calliope on those boats?

Well the piano player, that was up to him. When Lovingood was there he played it. When Steve Lewis was there he had to play it. When Professor Osceola Blanchard was there he had to play it. It was up to whatever piano player Sidney had, he had to play it. He had to go up there and play it.
Can you tell us anything about Steve Lewis since he's not living to talk to us? Can you tell us anything how he played or how was he on calliope?

Everybody enjoyed Steve Lewis' calliope playing. He played a, he played a, he plays a jazzy piano you know. And he played the calliope the same way he played the piano. Like he was like jazz music up on that calliope. The captain used to laugh every time he finished. But Steve didn't like that idea of playing up there. He said with that cotton in his ear and all that steam coming on him. Every time it's time for him to go think he said, Well let me, let me go up here and play this Don Hooper used to call it. He didn't call it the calliope he said. Let me go play this Hooper. Let me hurry up and get. He said I wish that half hour hurry up and pass. Cause I sure he had to go up there and fool with that thing. But otherwise the piano player he was a real, real, real good jazz man. You couldn't beat him. You couldn't beat him. See he played with Professor Piran for years. Up here at some country club in Jefferson Parish. They played up there for years. I think they played out of Spanish Fork. Oh yeah, yeah, yeah.
When did they play the calliope? Just before the boat would sail or how did they do that?

Well they played going into the town. Like if they're going into Memphis when they get about a mile out before they get to the land and he start playing it then. And then he'd go play it after dinner. Let them know the boat there. Then he'd play it and he'd get up there I imagine between 6, 6.30 or 7 or something like that. Just before the dance time. Let the people know the boat there. But you could hear that thing for miles though. Traveled. Those country places, these wide open spaces. Traveled. If you want to answer the phone.
No, he can answer.
Did you ever work any show boats?
When I was a kid I used to hear the calliopes on show boats too.
No sir, I didn't work no show boats. No sir, I didn't.
Did any of the river boats ever get the band out for any kind of a parade that you can remember?
No sir, not the Streckers Brothers. They don't believe in that.

Yeah. Because the show boats used to get out and turn it off. I was going to ask you to go back to Claiborne Williams again. Oh yeah. So many people have told us what a wonderful musician he was. But I've never even met any of his sons or anyone. If you can tell us any more. You mentioned how he taught you on breathing. Was any particular thing, was it using your diaphragm or deep breathing or what did he teach you?

Yeah, on how to take the breath. How to take your breath. Filling up the stomach. Filling up the stomach, surely, yeah. Just like those fellas who hold that note so long, you know? Yeah. That's what he was teaching me that.
Things like that.
The main particular thing. He has a son who's a wonderful musician also. By the name of George Williams, you ever heard of him?
Yes, I've heard of him. He was down here I think four or five years ago for a while.

He was. He played, he played, he played most all the instruments like his father. He played piano, trumpet, saxophone, beautiful tone in the saxophone. A wonderful musician. His sister, her name was Bella. Piano player, a wonderful piano player.

How was their band the dances? Did they play much really good dance music or was it sort of so much ranged and like, you know, waltzes and all? I mean, they didn't make a hot jazz, you know what I mean?

No, he didn't use that hot jazz. He just followed the stocks, you understand? And put in some waltzes. He had a beautiful waltz there, what he wrote there for his name, Logical Point. It's just beautiful waltz. That's when his brother used to play that. He used to play it way up above the staff. Every time he finished there, he had to lead him off the stand. He was weak, you see, from his lung trouble. But that man had a wonderful band. Just stocks, very few arrangements.
Did Claiborne Williams lead the band with the violin?
No, he played, very seldom professors played. Very seldom, very seldom he played.
Did he stand up with a baton or something?
No, he played, sit down and play. He let the trumpet player do the knocking off, you understand?
The trumpet player then?

Yeah, that was a fellow named Lawrence Hall. He was a wonderful trumpet player too. And he used to just sort of sit there, song his violin. He used to come to Pointville to give dances. He'd stay at the door and pick up the tickets, you understand? But he never would stand out in front of the band like that. Very seldom, I've never seen him stand out.
So I didn't know what kind of a band this was.

Joe Garbaro was the same way. He'd sit down and play his violin, he's a violin player too. And trumpet player used to do the knocking off, he'd just sit there, he'd just, if you'd watch him, he'd go right on to sleep. He used to go to sleep on you, you'd wake him up many times. When he'd be at the gambling table, he'd be playing cards, he'd sit right down there, fast asleep. Wake up Joe, what you got? He got like three kings in his head. He'd go, what you do, fast, sleeping. Yeah.
Where did Claiborne Williams teach? Was it at his home?

At his home, and he used to come down, all, if he got a, let's say like if he got a student in Bellrose, he'd come down there that day. If he got one in Pankoville, come down to Pointville to teach me, he made all he had that particular day to come, see? And then go back, but most of his teaching was at his home. He had more white pupils than he had color. Yeah.
Do you remember about what he charged for lessons?
50 cents.
50 cents.
50 cents.
How long did he last?
Oh, about a half hour, an hour. It's just, you see, when he come home, my dad would be at home, that's a long conversation. Sure. Many days I used to see him come and run hard. Why you hide?
You haven't done your lessons?
No, I hadn't gotten them.
Because he very strict, that is. Yeah, he's a strict, strict, strict fellow.
Yeah, he's strict. If he give you something, he wants you to have it.
Yeah, surely. Do you remember when you first learned to count,
how they taught you to count? Anything about counting or patting your foot?
Did you, did Claiborne Williams teach you to count with your foot?
Yeah, he always teaches you, one, two, three, four.
Sliding your foot on the side.
Up, down, slide over, yeah, that's right. See, that's the best way to count it. That's the way Adolf Alexander count. The same way.
Several people have told us they learned that way.
Yeah, that's the best way. Can't go wrong.
Yeah.

That's right. I come to the Bulls when, Sydney, we used to play up there every Tuesday night with Desvien. And they used to have so many people there, they used to have sometimes three bands. One used to play on this side for the yard, one on that, Sydney was on this side, Celestan was on that side, and René was in the middle. In the dance hall, you see, they had some people in there like that. Every Tuesday night you couldn't get in there. Two bands every Tuesday night. Some occasions they'd have three bands. Yeah, they, that.
I've never been in there, is that the upstairs? Downstairs.
Downstairs. Downstairs. The dance hall was downstairs, and the yard on this side and the yard on that side. We used to play on the yard on this side, and Celestan had that side.
All three bands playing at the same time?
Sure.
Yeah.

All the same time. People like that, you couldn't, you couldn't hear. You on that side you just go and hear Celestan, you come over this side you hear Desvien, you're in the hall, you're going to hear René. That's all you couldn't hear. Somebody would be outdoors in that big, big old space, yeah, big old yard they had. On Daniel Street. That's right, that's right. Sure.
Yeah, I didn't know that.
You didn't, huh?
They had the dances outdoors that way.

Now Joe Garbarale, you see, we used to, he used to have all down by Lafourche Lake, Golden Meadows, Lockport. Oh, a place way down by the name, by the fellow used to run it by the name of Luke. He had Homer, Schreiber, Tippett, he had all that part, the country tied up, Foyce, Lavertyville, and Cleven Williams had all the Mississippi River tied up, you understand, and Foyce would come down as far as Napoleonville. Yeah.
Who were the best trumpet players you ever heard in your life, would you say?
I liked Louis Armstrong myself.
I just wondered how Buddy Petit and Kid Renee compared with Louis?

Well to my judgment Buddy Petit was about, after Louis left here, he was about the best trumpet player around here. He was really good. He was a good jazz man. Buddy Petit was wonderful. To my opinion, maybe somebody might think differently. A lot of people told us that. Some of them, you know, I don't know. People have told us that. He was a little short fellow used to wear, wearing them stiff rimmed straw hats in the summertime and a brown derby in the wintertime. Yeah. Did he use his derby ever over the bell? No, he never used his derby. He used to put it down. No, he never did use his derby. Never did.
Did you ever use many mutes? Did you have this old band? Oh yeah, I had.
I had. When I was with Desvene, I had all the mutes. Cup mute. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Where did you get that way you have of accompanying the blues fingers?
It just came to me since Thomas gave me that cup. I never did use nothing like that. Thomas brought that there. I just fill in, that's all.
Well, didn't you ever do that anywhere before?
No.
Boy, it sounds fun.
You like it, huh? Yeah. I just fill in, that's all.
It works good, that way.
Oh yeah, sure.
What is it, a kettle?
I don't know what that is, Thomas brought that.
I think he says he's going to keep that order, he calls it or something.
I don't know what Thomas brought, I don't know where you get it from. I couldn't tell you.
Sounds fun, man. It works good.
Yeah, everybody likes it.
You probably make it talk, isn't it?
Yeah.
Funny sounds like it. When did you, how long have you been playing with Thomas now?
Oh, not so long, but I'd say roughly seven years. I don't think it's that long.
Yeah, seven years. So, were you with him at the Moulin Rouge before? I mean...

I got with him just at the closing. Oh, just at the closing now. I wasn't with him when he started there. He been over there about, played for spec about 12 years, you see. I wasn't there then. I came in just on the closing.
You've been with him ever since?
Ever since. I started with him just before I went in the post office. I'll be in there now six years. September. So I'd say about five years I've been with Thomas. Just about five. Yeah.
Yeah. And does it compare with, how does it compare with the other bands you play with such as, you know, like Buddy Petit or Kid Renee or Chris Kelly?

Well, all Dixieland bands to me compare the same way. They all gonna play the same numbers. They go, oh, it's always gonna give you that Dixieland beat. You know, you just sit down there and follow the drummer, that's all.
How do you like Sammy Stoner? Fine.
Fine. And what is your...
You got a nice beat. You got a nice beat.

Nice beat. What is your worst... I never did... I'm not too familiar with chords, you understand? Card forms. I'm not too familiar with that, but I got a good ear. When I was with Desveen I couldn't play like I was playing now. I could play melody, but I couldn't play that jazz, you understand? Get off. It just comes to me. I just hear the banjo, the piano, if he hitting that chord I can hear it. I know this way to fall, you see? Because I got a good ear. When I was with Desveen we play an orchestration down once, I don't need it no more. You have a good memory for music, but names and addresses and telephone numbers, you got me. If I don't write it down, that's it. All sitting and doing, I just have the book open in front of me, just turn the music. I don't need it because I memorize it, I know it. It's a funny thing. But names, if you don't write it down, that's it. You never hear from me no more. Can't memorize it.
I was going to ask about some of the brass bands, if you ever played much on, I've heard you over the last time.

Well just these around New Orleans, I forget the name of those bands, I say John Casimir. I don't know the name of his band, Eureka, isn't it? Young Tuxedo. Young Tuxedo and Poise Humphrey, he's Eureka, isn't it? Yeah, Eureka, yeah. That's the only two they have here I think, isn't it?
Well sometimes George Williams has had a band.

Well I played with him too. Dick Howard, different ones at times. Yeah, I played with Howard too, played with all of them, called himself one of the brass bands, played with all of them around there. You did mostly play for those clubs. Yeah, Mardi Gras. And Mardi Gras, well Mr. Bill I'm no young fella you see, and that walk was too much in that hot sun, I just couldn't make it too much. I played with them young trombone players, they'd come out there starting off, blowing a can, I tell them take it easy. See I know I'm like those old experienced ringer, old prize fighters in the ring. Round about one o'clock they, they slipping like that, then I come through and it's left up to me. See then I'll be out there by myself. Go ahead Jet, go in the back.
You got a cute dog there. Isn't it?
A little dog.
I just wondered if you'd ever played any regular brass bands or just a few filled in a few dates?
Just filled in me there was no regular. They weren't me regular, I could have played with Poise Humphrey there, what is it Tuxedo is there?
Eureka.

It is, well you see I'm handicapped with my job, driving trucks and force all the way, I work every Sunday. So that's mostly they have, the parades on Sunday so I had to turn them down. I had been offered but I just couldn't accept it.
We were talking about the, was it Pritchard's band or was it a symphony orchestra or something?

Pritchard he tried to arrange a symphony orchestra, yes sir. He was doing nicely with it. The Grand Lodge gave a session, I had the convention out in Shreveport. We went out there and played at that big auditorium, it sounded fine. And that night we played two nights out there for them. First night after we played the concert then they gave a dance. Well they didn't use all of them, they just used the Dixieland band. Pazjo was leading the band, you understand? We used about six pieces. Then the next day we went and played our last job at the auditorium and we played, the same band went back. We played for them that night for the dance. Then we left out that night after we danced by bus and moved back to New Orleans. But he had good ideas back there but people wouldn't stick. In other words the musicians that had the talent wouldn't go. He was trying to pick up those that wasn't up to it and try to make something out of it but couldn't make it.
I remember once you told me Mr. Blanchard, did you call him Professor of the Pianist?
Professor Arceola Blanchard. Is he still living? Yes sir he is. He's still teaching up at 35. Up at 35. That's on Gerard and Ramport. Oh yeah.
We tried to see him then.
I saw him a couple of days ago.
What is he teaching there?
Oh I don't know, I don't know if it's mathematics or English or I don't know what he teaches.
Well I thought he was teaching music up there but something else.
No, no. Other subjects. Yeah, he lived back in town someplace, I don't know.
We'll find out.
You can look in the telephone directly, I'm sure you'll find it. I'll see all of Blanchard.
Oh yeah.
On Zagra Street somewhere around in that neighborhood. Back of Copper Crystal Church back over there. See in that neighborhood. Oh yeah. You know his own home. Yeah. We'll find him all right.
Yeah. I wasn't sure if he was still there. Well you can go up by 35, he'll be there every day.
Yeah. Find him through that.
Mm-hmm. So is there anything else that you can think of about the button bands you played with that you skipped over? That's about it.
I played a session with Celestin. You know what I said? Played with him a couple of nights. You played Mardi Gras the year before last. What is that? With the Eureka band. Yes.
Oh yeah I remember singing Mardi Gras back in about 1949 I think. And I played with Kid Thomas I think last year we played on the flute. Oh yeah. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Day and night. I didn't have nothing, couldn't do nothing else. Then went to California, you know he died, you know. Yes, I know. We saw him there last year. We did, huh?
We talked to him a while.
He went out to California and I didn't hear any more from him. Man, just went to pieces.
Well, he looked quite well when I was there. He wasn't playing music anymore, but had a little restaurant.
Yeah, that's what I heard. My brother was out there, he said he met him.
Oh, do you have any other members of the family that played? I forgot to ask.
My brother played saxophone. He still played?
Did he ever play professionally around here much?

No, not too much, no. He didn't bother me as much. See, we both went in the Navy. I didn't have to go, but I took that opportunity and went as a musician, see. I came out, I went in as a musician second class, with a written, and I finished up musician first class. My reason for coming out when they passed that law when you was over forty-something I think it was, they let you go if you had an essential job. Well, at that time I was driving at the Port of Imbalcation. I had an essential job, so they discharged me.
Is your brother older or younger than you?
He's older. Older. He's born 1900. He'll be 60 in October. Can you think of anything, Ralph?
Well, is there any other members of your family like your son or your daughter? No, no, no, no, no.

They're going to take up music? No, no, no. It's me and my brother and my daddy, he's played piano too in organ. He used to play organ at the church in his spare time. Every sudden we'd go to church. He played organ and piano. He's not a fancy piano player but he played it. When he was out in the country he was a pretty good doctor. You had to use it on your own. See, the poor people are 80 miles from here. Just like this doctor come in here and rush to get the ambulance. No hospital out there. No, dirt roads, gravel, horse and bugger, no automobiles. You just had to know what you're doing. Or call in some other doctor to help you.
Didn't you say that Bunk Johnson knew Dr. Nelson?
I'm sure he did. He used to talk about it.
He used to talk about it.

segments.title: Birth in New Orleans, father the doctor, mother the pianist
segments.summary: Nelson gives his name and birthplace on Two Row Street, born 1902; father practiced medicine in Napoleonville; mother, a Boston Conservatory pianist, passed on the talent.

segments.title: First altos, then trombone lessons with Claiborne Williams
segments.summary: He started on alto horn around 16, admired his cousin's trombone playing, and learned breathing from Professor Williams; joined George Nelson's six-piece band.

segments.title: Country bands in Napoleonville area, then move to Kit Harris
segments.summary: Playing with Joseph Gabriel's ten-piece band and the James brothers in the country, getting his trombone at twenty and coming to New Orleans to join Kit Harris.

segments.title: Professor Claiborne Williams and his big band
segments.summary: Williams was a violinist who taught every instrument; his sixteen-piece stock-arrangement band played the Pelican roof garden, with his trombonist brother and son George.

segments.title: Joining Sidney Desvigne on the Streckfus boats
segments.summary: Eugene Ware recommended him to Desvigne; after a year of waiting he joined the orchestra on the Streckfus line and the Idlewild.

segments.title: Desvigne band personnel and hotel and club jobs
segments.summary: He names band members, then the hotel, restaurant and country club jobs, including Monday nights on the Pythian roof garden.

segments.title: Idlewild and other boats, Earl Humphrey leaving Desvigne
segments.summary: Bill and Nelson describe the Idlewild stern wheeler, trips upriver as far as Memphis, and trombonist Humphrey who left for show travel.

segments.title: Playing with Buddy Petit: head arrangements, style, cutting contests
segments.summary: Petit led a seven-piece head-arranging band, played close to Armstrong, was powerful, and met Rena in wagon contests.

segments.title: Kid Rena at the Lavida taxi dance hall
segments.summary: Rena was a soft, sweet trumpeter; the all-night gypsy dance job; band members including his drummer brother Joe Rena.

segments.title: One bad job with Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Kelly paid him in whiskey bottles on a job in the district, and Nelson vowed never to work with him again.

segments.title: Not playing the Storyville-district dance halls
segments.summary: He did not play the 101 Ranch or Pete Lala's but visited, and remembers Mr. Pena on drums.

segments.title: Best early trombonists and moving back to New Orleans in 1926
segments.summary: Question of best trombonists; Nelson moved back about 1926, and was the only trombonist in the country area.

segments.title: His first trombone and later horns
segments.summary: From a horn bought from Williams to a C.G. Conn and a Buescher with larger bore and bell, bought during WPA time.

segments.title: The WPA band under Professor Martinez
segments.summary: Martinez led a huge brass band favoring overtures; a trombone audition thinned it from 100 to 40 players, with names of members and small playing jobs.

segments.title: His mother's piano training and background
segments.summary: His mother taught school and played church organ; anecdote of her playing twelfth-grade music in a store; she came south teaching school.

segments.title: His father the doctor: schooling, practice and Spanish-American War
segments.summary: Dr. Nelson studied at Straight University, taught a surgeon, served as lieutenant at San Juan Hill, and is now old and deaf.

segments.title: Talk of earlier recordings in the Nelson home and absent drummers
segments.summary: They recall the room where recordings were made, musicians now gone, and trying to name a drummer who played with Big Eye.

segments.title: Streckfus captain, stock music and weekly rehearsals
segments.summary: Desvigne preferred stocks; the Streckfus captain timed the twelve numbers a night; rehearsals each Tuesday.

segments.title: Eleven weeks at St. Paul, Minnesota
segments.summary: Daily schedule of excursions and night dancing during the upriver stay.

segments.title: Boat pay, sleeping quarters and the President
segments.summary: Pay was $25 a week plus board; sleeping on the boats; a short stint on the President.

segments.title: Calliope playing on the boats and Steve Lewis
segments.summary: Piano players had to play the calliope; Steve Lewis played it jazzily and disliked it; when it was played; no show boat work.

segments.title: Williams's teaching of breathing, and his son George and daughter Bella
segments.summary: Williams taught breath control; son George was a multi-instrumentalist and Bella a pianist.

segments.title: Williams band style and violin-playing leaders
segments.summary: The band played stocks and waltzes, not hot jazz; leaders like Williams and Joe Gabriel sat and played violin while trumpeters knocked off.

segments.title: Lessons from Williams: fees, strictness and counting with the foot
segments.summary: Lessons cost fifty cents; Williams was strict and taught counting by foot-tapping.

segments.title: Three bands at the Bulls Club and Gabriel's territory
segments.summary: Desvigne, Celestin and Rena played simultaneously on Tuesday nights; Gabriel and Williams dominated country dance territory.

segments.title: Best trumpeters: Armstrong and Buddy Petit
segments.summary: He liked Armstrong; Petit was the best after Armstrong left; the mutes he used with Desvigne.

segments.title: The cup mute fill-ins with Kid Thomas
segments.summary: His accompaniment with a cup device that Thomas brought, which he plays to fill in.

segments.title: Time with Kid Thomas, playing by ear
segments.summary: About five years with Thomas, joining at the closing of the Moulin Rouge; Dixieland bands compare alike; he plays by ear and memorizes music.

segments.title: Brass band fill-ins and Mardi Gras
segments.summary: He filled in with Eureka and other brass bands but could not join regularly because of Sunday work.

segments.title: Pritchard's symphony orchestra and Professor Blanchard
segments.summary: The Grand Lodge convention job in Shreveport, and where pianist Blanchard now teaches.

segments.title: Playing with Celestin; a musician who went to California
segments.summary: He played a couple of nights with Celestin and the Eureka band, then talks about a musician who went to California.

segments.title: Brother and Navy service
segments.summary: His brother played saxophone; both joined the Navy as musicians and he was discharged for an essential job.

segments.title: Family musicians and his father the country doctor
segments.summary: Nobody in his children's generation took up music; his father played organ and was a country doctor, and Bunk Johnson knew him.
